 Employers to face cumulative fines for paying below minimum wage
 By Sam Garcia / Staff writer, with CNA 
 Add TT as Preferred Source 
 Fines for breaching minimum wage regulations would increase with each offense starting on Jan. 1, with penalties starting at NT$50,000 (US$1,523) for publicly listed companies and medical centers, the Ministry of Labor said today.
 The Taiwan Labor Front previously told a news conference that local governments lack standard penalties for when employers pay less than the minimum wage, with several places having no standards at all.
 These inconsistencies could undermine minimum wage protections, the group said, urging the ministry to coordinate with local governments to establish uniform penalty standards.
 The Ministry of Labor’s logo is displayed at the ministry in Taipei in an undated photograph. 
 Photo: Taipei Times
 The ministry today said that it has amended its guidelines for imposing fines under the Minimum Wage Act (最低工資法) and Labor Standards Act (勞動基準法) to ensure more consistent enforcement nationwide.
 The revisions introduce progressively higher fines for repeated contraventions and require local authorities to publish their penalty standards online.
 The amendments would take effect on Jan. 1 next year, it said.
 For specified major entities — including listed and over-the-counter companies, firms with paid-in capital exceeding NT$100 million and medical centers — fines for contraventions of key labor rules, including minimum wage and working hour requirements, would start at NT$50,000, the ministry said.
 Following coordination with local governments, the ministry said local authorities had agreed to use a three-year period when determining how many times an employer had contravened the same provision for calculating cumulative fines.
 Within that period, contraventions of the basic wage provisions under the Labor Standards Act and the Minimum Wage Act would be treated as contraventions of the same provision, the ministry said.
 Local governments would be required to publish their fine schedules, showing how penalties increase with repeated contraventions, on their official Web sites, it added.
 Workers who discover employers contravening labor laws or paying wages below the legal minimum wage can file complaints with local labor authorities or call the 1955 labor hotline, it said.

 Former China Central Television (CCTV) talk show host Cheng Wanjun (程萬軍) yesterday sought political asylum in Taiwan, a day after arriving at Taiwan Taoyuan International Airport on a connecting flight from Thailand.
In a video posted on X, Cheng said he was appealing to Taiwan to grant him temporary asylum on humanitarian grounds while he sought permanent resettlement in a third country.
Cheng said he previously served as editor-in-chief of the journal Law and Life and hosted legal affairs programs on state-run CCTV.
